summary: Extends the Routing Information Protocol (RIP) so its messages carry more useful information and add a measure of security. It obsoletes RFC 1388. It has been replaced by RFC 2453.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers swap simple notes about the best roads. This version lets the notes carry more detail and a secret handshake.

questions: difference between rip v1 and rip v2
subtitle: RIP gets subnet masks, next hops, route tags, multicast and a simple password, without breaking older routers.

tldr.problem: The original RIP message carries only the bare minimum for routing, with lots of unused space, no subnet mask and no authentication, which is a serious problem once networks are subnetted.
tldr.mechanism: RIP version 2 reuses the unused space in each 20-octet route entry for a route tag, a subnet mask and a next hop, uses an entry marked 0xFFFF for a simple password, and sends updates to the multicast address 224.0.0.9.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1723 was obsoleted by RFC 2453, so it is no longer the current definition of RIP version 2.

today: RFC 1723 is obsoleted by RFC 2453, which is the newer definition of RIP version 2. It itself obsoleted RFC 1388 and updated RFC 1058.

sections.title: Why Extend RIP
sections.content:
With newer routing protocols such as OSPF and IS-IS around, some people believed RIP was obsolete. The RFC argues otherwise: in a small network RIP has very little overhead in bandwidth, configuration and management time, and it is easy to implement. It also notes that there were many more RIP implementations in the field than OSPF and IS-IS combined.

The problem is the message itself. The existing RIP message holds the minimum needed for routing and a large amount of unused space. It predates autonomous systems, subnetting and authentication. The missing subnet mask is described as particularly serious: a router cannot tell whether a route with some non-network bits set is a subnet route or a host route, so some routers simply guess using the mask of the interface the route arrived on.
sections.plainLanguage: The old note was mostly empty space, and it forgot to say how big each neighbourhood was. Routers had to guess, so this version fills in the blanks.

sections.title: The RIP-2 Message Format
sections.content:
RIP version 2 does not change the protocol itself. It extends the message format. A message starts with a 4-octet header, followed by 1 to 25 route entries of 20 octets each. All fields are in network byte order (big-endian).

The Command, Address Family Identifier, IP Address and Metric keep the meanings from RFC 1058. The Version field is set to 2 for messages that use authentication or carry information in any of the newly defined fields. The two unused octets in the header are ignored.

The old unused space in each entry now holds three new fields: a route tag, a subnet mask and a next hop.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note keeps the same boxes as before, but the empty boxes now hold useful facts. The page is the same size, just fuller.

sections.title: Route Tag, Subnet Mask and Next Hop
sections.content:
The Route Tag is an attribute of a route that must be preserved and readvertised with it. Its intended use is to separate internal RIP routes from external ones imported from an EGP or another IGP. Routers that support other protocols should let the tag be configured per source, for example set to the number of the Autonomous System a route was learned from.

The Subnet Mask is applied to the IP address to give the non-host portion. A value of zero means no mask is included. Where RIP-1 routers may hear a RIP-2 entry, three rules apply: information internal to one network must never be advertised into another network, a more specific subnet may not be advertised where RIP-1 routers would treat it as a host route, and supernet routes must not be advertised where RIP-1 routers could misread them.

The Next Hop is the immediate address to which packets for the destination should be forwarded. 0.0.0.0 means route via the originator of the advertisement. The address must be directly reachable on the logical subnet used for the advertisement, otherwise it is treated as 0.0.0.0. It is only advisory: ignoring it can give a sub-optimal but valid route. Its purpose is to avoid extra hops, which helps when RIP is not run on all routers on a network. Appendix A shows an example where only one external router needs to speak RIP-2 with the internal routers.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag is a sticker saying where a road came from. The mask says how big the neighbourhood is. The next hop says, go ask that friend directly, it is quicker than going through me.

sections.title: Authentication and Multicast
sections.content:
Authentication is per message and needs more than the two octets available in the header, so it takes the space of a whole route entry. If the Address Family Identifier of the first entry, and only the first, is 0xFFFF, the rest of that entry carries authentication. That leaves at most 24 route entries. Currently the only Authentication Type is simple password, type 2: the remaining 16 octets hold a plain text password, left-justified and padded on the right with nulls (0x00).

A router configured to authenticate RIP-2 messages accepts RIP-1 messages and RIP-2 messages that pass the check, and discards unauthenticated or failed ones. A router not configured to authenticate discards authenticated RIP-2 messages. For maximum security, RIP-1 messages should be ignored when authentication is in use. A RIP-1 system ignores the authentication entry because it belongs to a non-IP address family, so authentication alone does not stop RIP-1 systems from seeing RIP-2 messages.

For periodic updates, RIP-2 uses the IP multicast address 224.0.0.9 so that hosts not listening to RIP-2 are not loaded. IGMP is not needed because these are inter-router messages that are not forwarded.
sections.plainLanguage: The first line of the note can hold a secret word, kept in a box 16 characters wide. Routers that expect the word throw away notes without it. Notes are also sent to a special group address, so only routers that care have to listen.

sections.title: Compatibility with RIP-1
sections.content:
RFC 1058 said that version 0 messages are discarded, version 1 messages are discarded if any must-be-zero field is non-zero, and messages of a higher version should not be discarded just because such a field is non-zero. So RIP-2 is backwards compatible with implementations that follow that rule.

Because some RIP-1 implementations do not follow it, and because multicast would keep RIP-1 systems from receiving updates, a per-interface compatibility switch is needed. It has four settings: RIP-1 (only RIP-1 messages sent), RIP-1 compatibility (RIP-2 messages broadcast), RIP-2 (RIP-2 messages multicast) and none (sending disabled). The recommended default is RIP-1 compatibility. A receive control switch should also allow RIP-1 only, RIP-2 only, both, or none.

A RIP-2 router that receives a RIP-1 request should answer with a RIP-1 response, unless it is configured to send only RIP-2 messages. The RFC also explains why infinity cannot be raised from 16: it would confuse older RIP versions, and shrinking the metric to one octet would break implementations that treat it as four octets. As in RIP-1, addressless links are not supported.
sections.plainLanguage: New routers still have to talk to old ones. A switch lets each connection choose to speak the old way, the new way, or both, so nobody gets left out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the basic RIP protocol is not secure. To bring RIP-2 in line with more modern routing protocols, it adds an extensible authentication mechanism, described in the authentication and compatibility rules above. The only type defined is a plain text password.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret word is written on the note in plain sight, so it keeps out strangers who are not looking, but it is not a vault.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Specifies version 2 for messages that use authentication or the new fields.

fields.name: Address Family Identifier
fields.desc: Same meaning as in RFC 1058; 0xFFFF in the first entry marks authentication.

fields.name: Route Tag
fields.desc: Preserved and readvertised with the route.

fields.name: Subnet Mask
fields.desc: Applied to the IP address; zero means no mask is included.

fields.name: Next Hop
fields.desc: Where to forward packets; 0.0.0.0 means via the originator.

fields.name: Command
fields.desc: Same as in an ordinary message.

fields.name: 0xFFFF
fields.desc: Marks the first entry as authentication.

fields.name: Authentication
fields.desc: 16 octets: plain text password, padded on the right with nulls.
